newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Bekaert share set to bounce after results.
newsitem.headline: Bekaert share set to bounce after results.

text.p: Shares in Belgian steel wire and cord maker Bekaert NV were hit so many times over the past year that they are likely to bounce after the company releases 1996 results on Wednesday, analysts said.
"All the bad news is in the share price. Any news that comes out is likely to be seen positively. The only question mark is the (1996) dividend," KB Securities analyst Pascale Weber said.

Bekaert was quoted at 21,750 Belgian francs at 1330 GMT on Tuesday, well below its year high of 33,000 francs hit on March 8, just before the first of three profit warnings in the space of nine months sent the share into a tailspin.

In the latest warning in December Bekaert said that net current earnings for 1996 would be "close to break-even" although group net profit would be boosted by a 2.3 billion franc capital gain from the sale of shares in Japan's Bridgestone Metalpha Corp.
The company announced a 2.911 billion franc plan to curb capacity in its European wire and cord plants, which it said would result in an aftertax charge in its 1996 accounts of 1.93 billion francs.
Analysts' estimates of current earnings per share (EPS) varied according to how the restructuring costs, which Bekaert is expected to book mostly against operating profit, were accounted for.
An Edinburgh Financial Publishing (EFP) survey of 12 analysts on Reuters Securities 3000 pegged 1996 EPS at 794 francs, down from 1,340 francs in 1995 and 2,886 in 1994.
Treating the restructuring costs as exceptional charge, Peter De Neve, an analyst with Bank Degroof, pegged 1996 EPS at 816 francs. BBL analyst Jean-Marie Caucheteux had EPS at around 766 francs.
Following Bekaert's own methodology of booking two thirds of the restructuring as charges against operating costs, KB Securities' Weber said EPS would represent a 15 francs loss.

All analysts noted that helped by the capital gain from the sale of the BMA shares and a smaller amount from the sale of Robotic Vision, the bottom line should show a positive result of 2.2 to 2.4 billion francs, down from 3.01 billion in 1995.
Analysts were divided on whether the cash from the BMA deal would be used to maintain the company's 1995 450 franc net dividend.
"It's possible to maintain it. They have the cash. But it would be more cautious to cut it to 350 francs," BBL's Caucheteux said.
Weber agreed, noting the company was in the "politically" difficult situation of laying off workers.
Degroof's De Neve expected the dividend to be maintained, or reduced only slightly.

"They could reduce it by say 10 percent, just to send the signal that they are asking a lot of their employees. That would not be negative for the share," he said. "On the other hand, if they reduce it more significantly it would be very negative."

Bekaert was expected to use its earnings presentation to underscore the positive impact the planned restructuring is expected to have on 1997 earnings and to emphasise once again the company's geographic diversification away from Europe, where overcapacity in its main products is greatest.
Bekaert said in February a major acquisition in Brazil to add to its existing businesses in Latin America. In July it announced new ventures in India and Indonesia.
Analysts said they were also looking for the company to dispel fears that Kevlar fibres for use in tyres developed by Du Pont could threaten Bekaert's steel cord products.
When adverts taken out by Du Pont in the Economist magazine were first noticed by the market last December they wiped five percent off Bekaert's already vulnerable share.
"(Kevlar) is still what is prompting a lot of uncertainty in the minds of investors," Degroof's De Neve said.
